title: London's free museums: do you need to book, and what does a paid audio tour add?
subtitle: Entry to the great national collections costs nothing. What you can pay for is a booked slot and a route.
excerpt: The British Museum, the National Gallery, the Natural History Museum, the Science Museum and Tate Modern are free. How the free timed tickets work, what is charged for inside, and what you really buy when a listing says reserved entry and audio tour.

what to see at the British Museum in two hours

which London museums are free
meta_title: London's free museums: booking, and paid audio tours
meta_description: London's national museums are free. How the free timed tickets work, what costs money inside, and what a paid reserved entry with audio tour adds.

featured_image.alt: The Great Court of the British Museum, with the round Reading Room under a glass and steel roof

content_html:
[place attraction="british-museum" city="london"]

Sir Hans Sloane, a London physician, spent his long life buying things: dried plants, coins, shells, manuscripts, antiquities, some 71,000 objects in all. When he died in 1753, his will offered the lot to the nation in exchange for a payment to his heirs far below its worth. Parliament accepted, and raised the money with a public lottery.

The British Museum opened on 15 January 1759, free of charge, to what its founding act called all studious and curious persons. Free did not mean easy. For decades a visitor had to apply in writing for a ticket and come back on the appointed day. Two and a half centuries later the great national museums of London still charge nothing at the door, and the visitor's question has returned in a new form: do you have to book, and what are you buying when someone sells you a ticket to a free museum?

What is free, and what is not

The permanent collections of the national museums are free for everyone, with no need to live in Britain or prove anything. Those most visitors want are:

  • the British Museum, in Bloomsbury;
  • the National Gallery, on Trafalgar Square;
  • the Natural History Museum, the Science Museum and the Victoria and Albert Museum, side by side in South Kensington;
  • Tate Modern, on the south bank of the Thames.

What costs money inside is the temporary exhibitions, which have their own timed tickets, and extras such as film shows and the museums' own audio guides. The boxes asking for a donation are a request, not a condition.

The National Gallery, across one of the fountains of Trafalgar Square. Photo: Ray in Manila, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Do you need to book?

Several of these museums offer a free timed ticket on their own websites, and recommend it. In most cases you can still walk up without one, and wait in a second line that is let in as space allows. On a wet Saturday or in the school holidays that line can be long at the British Museum and at the Natural History Museum. On a weekday morning in winter it hardly exists.

Three things to know:

  • A slot does not skip security. Bags are checked at the entrance, and that check is what the line really is.
  • Large luggage is refused. Suitcases and big rucksacks are not let in, so do not come straight from the station.
  • The second door is quieter. The British Museum has an entrance on Montague Place, at the back, and the Natural History Museum has one on Exhibition Road, round the corner from its main steps.

The rules on booking have changed several times in recent years. Look at our pages for the British Museum and the Natural History Museum before you go.

What a paid listing really is

If entry is free, a listing called reserved entry and audio tour is selling two things. The first is a service: somebody books the free slot for you. The second is the audio tour, a route through the building narrated in the partner's app on your own phone. You are not paying for admission, and the museum would give you the same slot for nothing.

  • British Museum: reserved entry and audio tour. A booked free slot and a route through the halls of about two hours.
  • National Gallery: reserved entry and audio tour with a city walk. A booked slot, commentary on the main paintings, and an audio walk through Westminster.
  • Natural History Museum: timed entry and audio tour with a Hyde Park walk. A booked slot, a route through the museum and a walk in the park.
  • Science Museum: timed entry and audio tour with a city walk. A booked slot and an audio tour that is largely a walk outside.
  • Tate Modern: audio tour. Commentary only. The listing itself says that admission is free.

Bring earphones and a charged phone. These are the museum listings our partner sells in London, with today's prices:

[partner city="london" match="british,gallery,natural,science,tate" limit="5"]

Is the audio tour worth paying for?

The British Museum has some eight million objects and shows a small part of them in more than sixty galleries. Without a plan most people drift through Egypt, get tired, and leave without having found what they came for. A route that takes you from one object to the next solves that.

If you would rather go at your own pace, a free map and a short list are enough. Here is one for two hours at the British Museum:

  • The Rosetta Stone, Room 4. The same decree in three scripts, which gave scholars the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs.
  • The Assyrian lion hunt reliefs, Room 10. Carved for a palace at Nineveh about 645 BC.
  • The Parthenon sculptures, Room 18. Brought from Athens by Lord Elgin in the first years of the nineteenth century, and argued over ever since.
  • The Egyptian mummies, Rooms 62 and 63, upstairs.
  • The Lewis Chessmen, Room 40. Chess pieces carved from walrus ivory in the twelfth century and found on a Scottish island.
  • The Sutton Hoo helmet, Room 41. From the ship burial of an Anglo-Saxon king, dug up in Suffolk in 1939.

The Rosetta Stone in its case, a few steps from the main entrance. Photo: APK, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

One thing to look for in each of the others

  • National Gallery. European painting from the thirteenth century to the early twentieth. Find the Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck, The Ambassadors by Holbein, with a stretched skull across its floor, and the Sunflowers of Van Gogh.
  • Natural History Museum. Alfred Waterhouse's building of 1881 is the first exhibit. In the central hall hangs the skeleton of a blue whale, which took the place of the cast of a Diplodocus in 2017.
  • Science Museum. The command module of Apollo 10, which flew round the Moon in 1969, and Puffing Billy, a steam locomotive built about 1813.
  • Victoria and Albert Museum. The Cast Courts, where a plaster copy of Trajan's Column stands in two halves because it is too tall for the room.
  • Tate Modern. A power station turned into a gallery, opened in 2000, with the Turbine Hall as its entrance.

The blue whale skeleton above the central hall of the Natural History Museum. Photo: APK, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The Turbine Hall of Tate Modern, once the engine room of a power station. Photo: Chris Whippet, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

When to go

The first hour after opening and the last ninety minutes of the day are the calmest. Weekends and school holidays are the worst, above all in South Kensington. Several museums stay open into the evening one day a week, often Friday, and those hours are quiet.

From here

The British Museum is ten minutes on foot from Covent Garden and fifteen from the National Gallery. From there, the river and Westminster are a short walk down Whitehall. Tate Modern faces St Paul's across the Millennium Bridge, and the Victoria and Albert Museum is next door to the other two in South Kensington. For the rest of London, or to fit it into a longer trip, open the trip planner for the United Kingdom.

Cover photo: Diliff, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Are the museums in London really free?
faqs.a: Yes. The permanent collections of the national museums, among them the British Museum, the National Gallery, the Natural History Museum, the Science Museum, the Victoria and Albert Museum and Tate Modern, are free for everyone. Temporary exhibitions are charged.

faqs.q: Do you need to book the British Museum in advance?
faqs.a: A free timed ticket is recommended and makes entry quicker on busy days, but in most cases you can still walk up and wait in the line for visitors without one. The rules change, so check before you go.

faqs.q: Why are tickets to free London museums sold online?
faqs.a: What is sold is a service and an audio tour: someone books the free slot for you, and you get a narrated route in an app on your phone. Admission itself is free.

faqs.q: Is an audio tour of the British Museum worth it?
faqs.a: It is useful if you want to be led from one famous object to the next without planning. If you prefer your own pace, a free map and a short list of rooms do the same job.

faqs.q: What can you see at the British Museum in two hours?
faqs.a: The Rosetta Stone, the Assyrian lion hunt reliefs and the Parthenon sculptures on the ground floor, then the Egyptian mummies, the Lewis Chessmen and the Sutton Hoo helmet upstairs.

title: Greenwich in a day: what is free, what needs a ticket, and how to get there
subtitle: A park, a palace, a museum and a view for nothing. A ship, a painted hall and the meridian line for a ticket each.
excerpt: How to spend a day in Greenwich: the boat, the train and the railway that get you there, the sights that are free, the three that need a ticket, and what the partner sells for the Royal Observatory, the Cutty Sark and the Painted Hall.
focus_keyword: Greenwich day trip from central London
longtail_phrases: what is free to do in Greenwich
do you have to pay to see the meridian line
how to get to Greenwich by boat
is the Cutty Sark worth it
how long do you need in Greenwich
meta_title: Greenwich in a day: what is free, what needs a ticket
meta_description: A day in Greenwich: how to get there by boat or train, what is free, and what the tickets for the Observatory, the Cutty Sark and the Painted Hall cover.

featured_image.alt: The view from the hill of Greenwich Park over the Queen's House and the Old Royal Naval College to the towers of Canary Wharf

content_html:
[place attraction="royal-observatory-greenwich" city="london"]

In 1675 King Charles II founded an observatory on a hill in his park at Greenwich, for one purpose: to find a way for ships to know how far east or west they were. Christopher Wren, who had been an astronomer before he was an architect, designed the house, and John Flamsteed, the first Astronomer Royal, spent more than forty years in it measuring the positions of the stars.

The charts made from that work spread to the ships of every nation. So when delegates of twenty-five countries met in Washington in October 1884 to agree on one line from which the world would count longitude, and with it the hours of the day, most of the world's shipping was already using Greenwich. Twenty-two voted for it, San Domingo voted against, France and Brazil abstained. The line runs through a courtyard on top of the hill, and standing on it needs a ticket. Much of what surrounds it does not.

Getting there

  • By boat. The river buses of Uber Boat by Thames Clippers run from Westminster, Embankment, London Bridge and Tower piers to Greenwich Pier. It is the slowest way and the best: you pass under Tower Bridge and arrive in front of the Old Royal Naval College, as its architects meant visitors to arrive.
  • By Docklands Light Railway. From Bank, through Canary Wharf, to the station called Cutty Sark, in the middle of everything.
  • By train. From London Bridge to Greenwich station in about ten minutes, then ten minutes on foot.
  • On foot under the river. A tunnel for walkers, opened in 1902, links Greenwich with Island Gardens on the north bank, where the view back to the college is the one Canaletto painted.

A common mistake: North Greenwich, with the O2 arena and the cable car across the Thames, is on a different bend of the river, a bus ride from the historic centre.

What is free

  • Greenwich Park and the view. From the statue of General Wolfe, beside the observatory, you look down on the Queen's House and the twin domes of the college, with the towers of Canary Wharf behind.
  • The Queen's House. Designed by Inigo Jones, begun in 1616: the first building in England in the classical manner he had studied in Italy. Go in for the Tulip Stairs, a spiral with no central support, and the Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I.
  • The National Maritime Museum. Among much else it keeps the coat Nelson wore at Trafalgar, with the hole made by the musket ball in the left shoulder.
  • The grounds and the chapel of the Old Royal Naval College. Wren planned it in the 1690s as a hospital for old sailors. It stands in two halves because Queen Mary insisted that the Queen's House keep its view of the river.
  • Greenwich Market, under its roof between the college and the park, for lunch.

The red time ball on Flamsteed House. It has dropped at one o'clock since 1833. Photo: MrsEllacott, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What needs a ticket

The Royal Observatory

The ticket covers Flamsteed House, the Meridian Courtyard with the line set into the paving, and the sea clocks of John Harrison, the carpenter who solved the longitude problem with a watch. The meridian is not an arbitrary stripe: it is the line of sight of a telescope, the Airy Transit Circle of 1851, which is still in its room. A satellite receiver puts zero about a hundred metres further east, in the park, because the modern system measures from the centre of the Earth.

The red ball on the roof has been dropped at one o'clock every day since 1833, so that ships in the river could set their clocks. You can watch it from the park for nothing. The observatory has been carrying out building works, and the planetarium has its own ticket: check what is open on our page for the Royal Observatory.

The meridian marked on the wall of the building that houses the telescope which defines it. Photo: Chris Gorringe, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

The Cutty Sark

A tea clipper launched at Dumbarton in 1869, the year the Suez Canal opened and made her kind of ship obsolete. She found a second life carrying wool from Australia, and in 1885 ran from Sydney to London in 73 days. A fire during restoration in 2007 destroyed less than was feared, because much of her timber had been taken away for the works. Since 2012 the hull has been raised three metres inside a glass enclosure. The ticket lets you walk the decks and the hold, and then stand underneath the keel.

The masts of the Cutty Sark, a minute from the pier. Photo: DiscoA340, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Painted Hall

The dining hall of the sailors' hospital, which James Thornhill painted from floor to ceiling between 1707 and 1726. It turned out too grand for the pensioners to eat in. Nelson's body lay in state here in January 1806. The hall is the one part of the Old Royal Naval College that needs a ticket.

The Painted Hall, lit by the lamps on its tables. Photo: Colin Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • Royal Observatory Greenwich entry. The entrance ticket and nothing else. No audio guide is part of it.
  • Greenwich sightseeing walk with Royal Observatory ticket. The same entry, with an audio walk through the town and the park in the partner's app. The commentary stops at the door: it does not cover the inside of the observatory.
  • Cutty Sark entry. The entrance ticket to the ship.
  • Maritime gems with Cutty Sark ticket. Entry to the ship with an audio walk past the college, the museum and the park. Again, the audio is for the streets, not the ship.
  • A river boat ticket with the Painted Hall. A crossing on the river bus bundled with entry to the hall. It is sold as a single trip and as a return, so check which one you are looking at.

These are the Greenwich tickets and audio walks our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="london" match="greenwich,observatory,cutty,painted" limit="5"]

A day in order

Take a morning boat and begin with the Cutty Sark, which is a minute from the pier. Cross to the college for the Painted Hall and the chapel opposite it. Eat at the market. In the afternoon walk through the Maritime Museum and the Queen's House, which leave you at the foot of the park, and climb the hill last, when the light falls on the river. If you want to see the ball drop, turn the day round and be on the hill before one.

The three paid sights take about an hour each. If you want only one, choose by taste: the observatory for the idea, the ship for children, the hall for painting.

From here

The boat back to the centre passes Canary Wharf and the Tower, and at dusk it is worth the fare for itself. Hours for the Cutty Sark, the National Maritime Museum and the Queen's House are on their pages. See what else there is in London, or open the attractions map of the United Kingdom.

Cover photo: Txllxt TxllxT, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: What is free to do in Greenwich?
faqs.a: Greenwich Park and its view, the Queen's House, the National Maritime Museum, the grounds and the chapel of the Old Royal Naval College, and the market are all free.

faqs.q: Do you have to pay to stand on the meridian line?
faqs.a: The line in the Meridian Courtyard is inside the Royal Observatory, which needs a ticket. The park around it, the view and the daily drop of the time ball can be seen for nothing.

faqs.q: How do you get to Greenwich from central London?
faqs.a: By river bus from Westminster, Embankment, London Bridge or Tower pier to Greenwich Pier, by Docklands Light Railway to Cutty Sark station, or by train from London Bridge to Greenwich in about ten minutes.

faqs.q: How long do you need in Greenwich?
faqs.a: A full day if you want the Cutty Sark, the Painted Hall, the museums and the observatory. Half a day is enough for the park, the view and one paid sight.

faqs.q: Is the Cutty Sark worth visiting?
faqs.a: It suits families and anyone interested in ships: the ticket lets you walk the decks and the hold, then stand under the hull, which is raised three metres above the floor of its dock.

title: Walking the Royal Mile in Edinburgh: what is free, and what needs a ticket
subtitle: One street, five names, a castle at the top and a palace at the bottom. Walk it downhill and know where to pay.
excerpt: How to walk the Royal Mile in Edinburgh from the castle to the Palace of Holyroodhouse: the free stops, the three sights that need a ticket booked ahead, and what the partner sells along the street.
secondary_keywords: what is free on the Royal Mile
longtail_phrases: how long does it take to walk the Royal Mile
what is free on the Royal Mile in Edinburgh
do you need to book Edinburgh Castle in advance
is the Stone of Destiny still in Edinburgh Castle
which end of the Royal Mile to start
meta_title: Walking the Royal Mile: what is free, what needs a ticket
meta_description: The Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle down to Holyroodhouse: the free stops, the sights to book ahead, and what the partner's tickets and audio walks cover.

featured_image.alt: The High Street of the Royal Mile in Edinburgh, lined with tall stone tenements, with the crown spire of St Giles' in the distance

content_html:
[place attraction="edinburgh-castle" city="edinburgh"]

The rock under Edinburgh Castle is the plug of a volcano that went cold some 350 million years ago. When the ice sheets moved across it from the west, the hard rock split the flow and sheltered a long tail of softer ground behind it. That tail, a ridge sloping gently east for well over a kilometre, is the street now called the Royal Mile.

A town built on a ridge cannot spread sideways. Hemmed in by its wall, and by a marshy loch where Princes Street Gardens are today, old Edinburgh grew upwards instead: tenements of eight, ten and more storeys, with the alleys called closes dropping steeply between them. The street is still one continuous line from the castle to the palace, and it is free to walk. What a visitor needs to know is which of the doors along it are free as well, and which three need a ticket bought before the day.

One street, five names

The Royal Mile is a nickname. On the map it is Castlehill, then the Lawnmarket, the High Street, the Canongate and, for the last few metres, Abbey Strand. The Canongate was a separate town until 1856, which is why it has a tolbooth and a church of its own. The length is about a Scots mile, an old measure longer than the English one: roughly 1.8 kilometres.

Walk it downhill, from the castle to the palace. Without stopping it takes twenty-five minutes. With the stops below it fills a day.

The castle from the esplanade, which is as far as you get without a ticket. Photo: Daniel Kraft, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What is free, from the top down

  • The castle esplanade. The parade ground in front of the gate, with views north and south over the city. In summer it is filled by the grandstands of the military tattoo.
  • The Writers' Museum. In Lady Stair's Close, off the Lawnmarket: a house of 1622 given over to Burns, Scott and Stevenson.
  • St Giles' Cathedral. The town church, where John Knox preached. Entry is free, with a donation asked. See the Thistle Chapel, a small room of carved oak finished in 1911.
  • The Heart of Midlothian. A heart set in the cobbles beside St Giles', on the site of the old prison. Local people spit on it for luck, so do not stand on it.
  • The closes. Step into any that is open. Advocate's Close frames the view north, and Dunbar's Close, on the Canongate, hides a garden laid out in seventeenth-century style.
  • The Museum of Edinburgh and the Canongate Kirk. The city's own museum, in a sixteenth-century house, and across the street the churchyard where the economist Adam Smith is buried.
  • The Scottish Parliament. The building by Enric Miralles, opened in 2004, at the foot of the street. Visitors can go in on most days.

The crown spire of St Giles', finished about 1495. Photo: Tony Hisgett, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Canongate Tolbooth of 1591, on the lower half of the street. Photo: rboed, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The three sights to book ahead

Edinburgh Castle

Entry is by ticket for a fixed time, and in summer the day's tickets are often gone before the morning is over. Book on the castle's own site, days ahead in July and August, and take the first slot: the street behind you is empty at that hour. Allow two hours inside for the Crown Room with the Honours of Scotland, the Great Hall, the twelfth-century chapel of St Margaret, which is the oldest building in the city, and the gun fired at one o'clock on most days.

One correction to older guidebooks: the Stone of Destiny, on which Scottish kings were crowned, is no longer in the Crown Room. It moved to the new museum in Perth in 2024.

The Real Mary King's Close

In the 1750s the city built its Royal Exchange, now the City Chambers, on top of several closes, using the lower storeys of the old houses as foundations. The streets survive underneath. They are visited only on a guided tour of about an hour, in small groups at fixed times, with steep steps and low ceilings. The evening and weekend tours sell out first.

The Palace of Holyroodhouse

The King's official residence in Scotland. The visit goes through the state rooms to the chambers of Mary, Queen of Scots, where her secretary David Rizzio was stabbed to death in 1566, and out into the roofless nave of the abbey founded in 1128. The palace closes to visitors when the King is in residence, usually for a week around the start of July, and on other dates through the year: see our page for the Palace of Holyroodhouse.

The entrance of the Palace of Holyroodhouse, at the foot of the Royal Mile. Photo: Daniel Kraft, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Reading the partner's listings

Our partner sells no ticket to Edinburgh Castle. Listings with the castle in their name are audio tours told from outside the gate, and one of them is still named after the Stone of Destiny.

  • Palace of Holyroodhouse ticket and Royal Mile walk. Entry to the palace, with an audio walk down the street in the partner's app. The commentary does not cover the inside of the palace.
  • The Real Mary King's Close entry ticket. A place on the guided tour under the City Chambers.
  • King's Gallery ticket and sightseeing audio tour. The King's Gallery is the exhibition space beside the palace, with changing shows from the Royal Collection. It is not the palace, and the two are easy to confuse.
  • Audio walks of the Royal Mile and the Old Town. Commentary and a map on your phone. No entry to anything is included.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells along the Royal Mile, with today's prices:

[partner city="edinburgh" match="royal mile,old town,holyrood,mary king" limit="6"]

Practical notes

  • The street is cobbled in parts, and the closes are stairs. Wear shoes with a grip, above all in the rain.
  • In August the festivals fill the High Street with performers and the pavements barely move. Walk early, or after six.
  • Going downhill, the palace is the natural end. Check its last admission before you linger at the top.

From here

Behind the palace rises Holyrood Park, with the path up Arthur's Seat, another dead volcano and the best view of the ridge you have just walked. Back up the hill, the National Museum of Scotland is free and five minutes south of St Giles'. Hours for the castle are on its page. For the rest of Edinburgh, or a longer route north, open the trip planner for the United Kingdom.

Cover photo: Anthony O'Neil, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk the Royal Mile?
faqs.a: About twenty-five minutes downhill without stopping: the street is roughly 1.8 kilometres long. With the castle, the closes, St Giles' and the palace it fills a whole day.

faqs.q: What is free on the Royal Mile?
faqs.a: The castle esplanade, St Giles' Cathedral, the Writers' Museum, the Museum of Edinburgh, the closes, the Canongate churchyard and the Scottish Parliament can all be visited without a ticket.

faqs.q: Do you need to book Edinburgh Castle in advance?
faqs.a: Yes, in the busy months. Entry is by ticket for a fixed time and summer days sell out, so book on the castle's own site days ahead and take an early slot.

faqs.q: Is the Stone of Destiny still in Edinburgh Castle?
faqs.a: No. It moved to the new museum in Perth in 2024. The Honours of Scotland, the crown, sceptre and sword, are still shown in the Crown Room of the castle.

faqs.q: Which end of the Royal Mile should you start at?
faqs.a: Start at the castle and walk downhill to the Palace of Holyroodhouse. The castle is quietest in its first slot of the day, and the slope is with you all the way.

title: Walking York's city walls: the route, how long it takes, and what is free
subtitle: Two miles of medieval wall, four gates, three gaps, no ticket. Which way round, and which stretch if you have half an hour.
excerpt: How to walk the city walls of York: the full circuit gate by gate, the best short section, when the walls are closed, and which sights nearby are free and which need a ticket.
secondary_keywords: how long to walk York walls
longtail_phrases: how long does it take to walk York city walls
are the York city walls free
where to start the York walls walk
which is the best section of York city walls
can you walk all the way round York walls
meta_title: Walking York's city walls: route, time, what is free
meta_description: York's medieval walls are free and take about two hours to walk. The circuit gate by gate, the best half hour, and what costs money nearby.

featured_image.alt: The towers of York Minster rising above brick buildings and gardens, seen from the city walls

content_html:
[place attraction="york-city-walls" city="york"]

In 1800 the corporation of York asked Parliament for leave to pull down the city walls. They had been useless in war for a century and a half, they cost money to patch, and the gates were so narrow that coaches jammed in them. The plan came to nothing, but for the next thirty years the corporation took pieces down anyway: three of the four barbicans, several of the smaller gates, stretches of the wall itself.

What stopped it was a public campaign, one of the first of its kind in England. Its loudest voice was the painter William Etty, born in York, who wrote letter after letter in defence of the gates. By the middle of the century the city was paying to repair what it had tried to remove. The result is the longest circuit of medieval town walls in England, and one of the few great sights in the country that asks no ticket. The questions are how to walk it, and how much of it.

The walls in numbers

The circuit is about 3.4 kilometres, a little over two miles. Most of the stonework is of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, raised on earth banks older than the Norman conquest, and in one corner on the wall of the Roman fortress. There are four main gates, which in York are called bars, while the streets are called gates: Micklegate Bar, Bootham Bar, Monk Bar and Walmgate Bar.

A full round takes about two hours at an easy pace. The path is on top of the wall, narrow in places, with a parapet on the outer side. On the inner side there is a railing only in places.

The walkway on top of the walls, with the grass rampart falling away beside it. Photo: Tim Green, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The circuit, gate by gate

If you arrive by train, the wall is facing you as you leave the station. Climb the steps there and go clockwise.

From the station to Bootham Bar

The wall runs down to the river Ouse with the Minster ahead of you the whole way, the view on every postcard. It stops at Lendal Bridge. Cross the bridge and go through the Museum Gardens, where the Multangular Tower shows the corner of the Roman fortress: small neat stones with a band of red tile below, larger medieval blocks above.

Bootham Bar to Monk Bar

The best quarter of an hour of the walk. Bootham Bar stands where the north-west gate of the Roman fortress stood. From it the wall turns behind the Minster, above walled gardens that you cannot see from any street, with the whole length of the cathedral beside you. It comes down at Monk Bar, the tallest of the four, which still has its portcullis.

Monk Bar to Walmgate Bar

A quieter stretch, ending at a real gap. Here the Normans dammed the river Foss and made a wide marshy pool that defended the town by itself, so no wall was ever built. Follow the road beside the Foss to the Red Tower, a small brick tower of 1490, where the wall begins again and leads to Walmgate Bar. This is the only gate in England that kept its barbican, the walled passage in front that forced attackers into a trap. The scars on it date from the siege of 1644.

Walmgate Bar, the only gate that still has its barbican. Photo: Chabe01, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Walmgate Bar to Micklegate Bar

The wall passes Fishergate, then breaks again at the castle. Walk past Clifford's Tower, cross the Ouse by Skeldergate Bridge and climb back up. The last section leads to Micklegate Bar, the gate by which kings entered the city and above which the heads of traitors were displayed. In 1460 one of them was Richard, Duke of York, wearing a paper crown. A few minutes more bring you back to the station.

Micklegate Bar, the gate by which kings entered York. Photo: Tim Green, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

If you have half an hour

Walk from Bootham Bar to Monk Bar, then come back at street level through the Minster's precinct. If you have ten minutes before a train, climb the steps opposite the station and walk towards the river and back. In March and April the banks below that stretch are yellow with daffodils.

Rules, and when the walls are closed

  • The walls are free, and open from about eight in the morning until dusk. The gates at the foot of the steps are locked at night.
  • They are closed when there is ice or snow, and sometimes in high winds. The stone is slippery when wet.
  • Every access is by steps, some of them steep and narrow. There is no route for wheelchairs or pushchairs.
  • Keep hold of small children: the inner edge is open in many places.
  • Dogs are not allowed on the walls, apart from assistance dogs.
  • In the gaps, small brass markers set in the pavement show the way to the next section.

What costs money in York, and what does not

  • Free: the walls, the Museum Gardens with the ruins of St Mary's Abbey, the Shambles, the street of overhanging butchers' houses, and the National Railway Museum behind the station, which holds Mallard, the locomotive that set the world speed record for steam in 1938.
  • With a ticket: York Minster, which charges visitors outside service times, with the climb of its central tower sold separately. Also Clifford's Tower, the keep of the castle, the Jorvik Viking Centre, the York Castle Museum and the York Dungeon.

Clifford's Tower, the keep of York Castle, on its mound. Photo: Chabe01, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

Nobody sells a ticket to the walls, because there is none. What our partner has in York is this:

  • National Railway Museum timed entry and audio tour with a city walk. The museum is free. The listing gives you a booked free slot, a narrated route through its halls in the partner's app, and an audio walk through the city that takes in the walls.
  • An audio tour of York through its history. A walk of about two hours past the Minster, the Shambles and Clifford's Tower. No entry tickets are part of it.
  • A ghost stories audio tour. The same streets after dark, with the legends. No tickets either.
  • York Dungeon entry ticket. A show with actors about the grim side of the city's past. It is an attraction of its own and has nothing to do with the walls.

[partner city="york" match="york" limit="6"]

From here

From Bootham Bar it is two minutes to the west door of York Minster. The National Railway Museum is behind the station, and the York Castle Museum stands beside Clifford's Tower, where the circuit breaks. York is about two hours from London by train and two and a half from Edinburgh, so it works as a stop between the two. Hours for the walls are on our page for the York city walls. See what else there is in York, or open the attractions map of the United Kingdom.

Cover photo: Oscar Taylor, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

faqs.q: How long does it take to walk York city walls?
faqs.a: About two hours for the full circuit of roughly 3.4 kilometres, including the three places where you come down to street level. The best short section, from Bootham Bar to Monk Bar, takes a quarter of an hour.

faqs.q: Are the York city walls free?
faqs.a: Yes. There is no ticket and no booking. The walls are open from about eight in the morning until dusk and are closed in ice, snow and sometimes high winds.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to start the York walls walk?
faqs.a: If you come by train, at the steps opposite the station, going clockwise towards the river with the Minster ahead. Otherwise start at Bootham Bar, beside the Minster.

faqs.q: Can you walk all the way round York on the walls?
faqs.a: Almost. The wall is missing in three places: at Lendal Bridge, along the river Foss, where a marshy pool once defended the town, and at the castle. Brass markers in the pavement show the way between the sections.

faqs.q: Are the York city walls suitable for pushchairs or wheelchairs?
faqs.a: No. Every access is by steps, the path is narrow, and the inner edge has no railing in many places.

title: The Beatles in Liverpool: which sites are free, which need a ticket, and how to reach them
subtitle: Half of them are in the city centre and half are in the southern suburbs. Plan the two halves separately.
excerpt: The Beatles sites of Liverpool in two groups: Mathew Street, the Pier Head and the museums in the centre, then Penny Lane, Strawberry Field and the childhood homes in the suburbs. What is free, what needs a ticket, and how to get between them.
secondary_keywords: how to get to Penny Lane

featured_image.alt: The bronze statue of the four Beatles walking along the waterfront at the Pier Head in Liverpool

content_html:
[place attraction="liverpool-beatles-museum" city="liverpool"]

On Saturday 6 July 1957 the parish church of St Peter, in the Liverpool suburb of Woolton, held its summer fete. Among the attractions was a skiffle group of schoolboys called the Quarrymen, who played from the back of a lorry and then in a field behind the church. Their singer was sixteen and his name was John Lennon.

That evening, while the group set up for a dance in the church hall across the road, a friend brought over a boy of fifteen who could tune a guitar and knew all the words to the songs. Paul McCartney joined the group a few weeks later. The hall and the church are still there, and they show the difficulty of a Beatles day in Liverpool: the places where the story happened are ordinary streets, eight or nine kilometres from the city centre, while the museums that tell it are by the waterfront. You need a plan for each half.

In the city centre, on foot

Free

  • Mathew Street. A narrow lane of old fruit warehouses. The Beatles played the Cavern Club here 292 times between February 1961 and August 1963. The original cellar was closed in 1973 and filled in during work on the underground railway. The club you enter today was rebuilt in 1984 on part of the same site, reusing bricks from the old one. It charges a small entry fee at some hours.
  • The statue at the Pier Head. The four of them, larger than life, walking towards the river. It was put up in 2015, fifty years after their last concert in the city.
  • Eleanor Rigby. A bronze figure on a bench in Stanley Street, round the corner from Mathew Street.
  • The Museum of Liverpool. The city's own museum at the Pier Head, free, with a section on its music.

Mathew Street, where the Cavern Club was and is. Photo: Stephen McKay, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

With a ticket

  • The Beatles Story, at the Royal Albert Dock. The large one: a walk through rebuilt scenes, from Hamburg to Abbey Road, with an audio guide.
  • The Liverpool Beatles Museum, on Mathew Street. Several floors of original objects, instruments, clothes and letters, collected by the family of Pete Best, the drummer before Ringo Starr.
  • The British Music Experience, in the Cunard Building at the Pier Head. British pop music since 1945 as a whole. The Beatles are one chapter of it, not the subject.

In the suburbs

Free

  • Penny Lane. A real street, and the name of the district around the junction at its top end, where the bus shelter in the middle of the roundabout and the barber's shop of the song still stand. The street signs were stolen so often that the council took to painting the name on the walls.
  • The gates of Strawberry Field. On Beaconsfield Road, in Woolton. Strawberry Field was a Salvation Army children's home whose wooded grounds Lennon climbed into as a boy. The red gates on the road are copies, and you can stand in front of them without paying.
  • St Peter's churchyard. A gravestone here carries the name Eleanor Rigby. McCartney has said he made the name up, and may have seen it here without remembering.
  • The two houses, from the pavement. Mendips, at 251 Menlove Avenue, where Lennon lived with his aunt Mimi from 1945 to 1963, is five minutes on foot from Strawberry Field. McCartney's family home, 20 Forthlin Road, is about a mile away.

One of the Penny Lane signs, painted on the wall because the metal ones kept being taken. Photo: Rept0n1x, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

The red gates of Strawberry Field, on Beaconsfield Road. Photo: Rodhullandemu, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

With a ticket

  • Strawberry Field. Behind the gates the Salvation Army opened a visitor centre in 2019, with an exhibition about the home and the song, and the garden.
  • Inside the two houses. Both belong to the National Trust and are furnished as they were in the 1950s. They are seen only on the Trust's own guided tour, by minibus, in small groups. Places are few and go weeks ahead. You cannot knock on the door, and people live in the neighbouring houses.

Mendips, 251 Menlove Avenue, John Lennon's home from 1945 to 1963. Photo: Rodhullandemu, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

How to reach the suburbs

  • By bus. Frequent city buses run from the centre along Smithdown Road to the Penny Lane junction in about twenty minutes. From there to Strawberry Field is three kilometres, a pleasant walk across Calderstones Park, or another short bus ride.
  • By tour coach. The Magical Mystery Tour, a two-hour coach trip, leaves from the Royal Albert Dock, stops for photographs at Penny Lane, Strawberry Field and outside the houses, and ends at the Cavern.
  • By taxi. Several firms run Beatles tours in black cabs, which can stop where a coach cannot. Agree the route and the length first.

None of these takes you inside the houses. Only the National Trust tour does.

Reading the partner's listings

  • Liverpool Beatles Museum entry ticket. Entry to the museum on Mathew Street.
  • Strawberry Field entry ticket. Entry to the visitor centre and garden in Woolton. Getting there is up to you.
  • British Music Experience entry ticket. Entry to the museum at the Pier Head.
  • Two audio walks of the centre, one on the maritime city and one on the waterfront. Both pass the Pier Head and the Cavern Club, with commentary in the partner's app. No entry tickets are part of them.
  • A listing that pairs Anfield stadium with a city audio tour is about football, and its list of inclusions mentions only the audio tour. Read what is written before you pay.

These are the tickets and audio walks our partner sells in Liverpool, with today's prices:

[partner city="liverpool" match="beatles,strawberry,music,maritime,waterfront" limit="6"]

How much time

One day covers both halves. Spend the morning in the suburbs, when the pavements at Penny Lane and the gates are empty, and come back to the centre for a museum and Mathew Street in the afternoon. With half a day, stay in the centre and choose one museum: The Beatles Story for the whole tale told in order, the museum on Mathew Street for real objects.

Liverpool is a little over two hours from London by direct train and under an hour from Manchester. Lime Street station is ten minutes on foot from Mathew Street.

From here

The Beatles Story sits among the brick and iron warehouses of the Royal Albert Dock, opened in 1846. The Museum of Liverpool is next to them on the waterfront, and the ferry across the Mersey leaves from the landing stage in front of it. Hours for the Liverpool Beatles Museum are on its page. For the rest of Liverpool, or a route through the north of England, open the trip planner for the United Kingdom.

faqs.q: Which Beatles sites in Liverpool are free?
faqs.a: Mathew Street, the statue at the Pier Head, the Eleanor Rigby statue, Penny Lane, the gates of Strawberry Field, St Peter's churchyard in Woolton and the outside of the two childhood homes can all be seen without a ticket.

faqs.q: How do you get to Penny Lane from Liverpool city centre?
faqs.a: Frequent city buses along Smithdown Road reach the Penny Lane junction in about twenty minutes. Coach and taxi tours from the centre also stop there.

faqs.q: Can you go inside John Lennon's and Paul McCartney's childhood homes?
faqs.a: Only on the National Trust's own guided tour, which goes by minibus in small groups and has to be booked well ahead. Other tours stop outside on the pavement.

faqs.q: Is the Cavern Club in Liverpool the original?
faqs.a: Not exactly. The original cellar closed in 1973 and was filled in. The present club was rebuilt in 1984 on part of the same site in Mathew Street, reusing bricks from the old one.

faqs.q: How long do you need for the Beatles sites in Liverpool?
faqs.a: One full day for both the suburbs and the centre. With half a day, stay in the centre and visit one museum and Mathew Street.
